title: G major and key signatures
summary: Start the pattern on G, find why it needs F sharp and write that once at the start.

hook.text: Start the ladder on G instead, staying on the white keys. Press play and compare the top with the C ladder. Does it still sound like an arrival?

explore.text: Start on G and climb with the pattern: [[tone|tone]], [[tone|tone]], [[semitone|semitone]], then [[tone|tone]], [[tone|tone]], [[tone|tone]], [[semitone|semitone]]. Check each step on the keys. Near the top, one white key will not fit the pattern, and a black key will.
explore.goal: Play G up to the next G, following the pattern all the way.

cards.text: E up to F is a [[semitone|semitone]], but the pattern wants a [[tone|tone]] there. Raise F to F♯ with a [[sharp|sharp]] and every step fits: G, A, B, C, D, E, F♯, G. The scale of G major has one sharp, F♯.

A piece built from the notes of G major is in the [[key|key]] of G major. Writing ♯ before every F would be tiring, so the sharp is written once, at the start of the [[stave|stave]], after the [[clef|clef]]. That is the [[key-signature|key signature]].

Read it like this. No signs means C major. One sharp, on the top line, means G major. Every F is now F♯, in every [[octave|octave]], even with no sign beside it. Look at [[bar|bar]] 3 below: that F♯ has no sign of its own.

alternative.text: Think of a key signature as a label on a box of notes. The box marked with one sharp holds F♯ instead of F. Reach in for any F and you pull out F♯. The unmarked box is C major. On the keyboard, the black key next to F, on its right, is the one in the box.

questions.prompt: One clip is a proper G major scale. The other uses a plain F. Which clip is G major?
questions.hint: Listen to the last step up to the top G. In a major scale it is a tight little step.

options.reason: Clip B uses a plain F, so the small step comes too early and the last step up to G is a big one. The top does not feel like an arrival. Clip A has F♯.

questions.prompt: What does F♯ fix in the scale of G major?
questions.hint: The pattern needs a [[tone|tone]] after E and a [[semitone|semitone]] next to the top note.

face.text: It makes every note in the scale sharp.

options.reason: Only F is sharp. The other six notes of G major are plain white keys.

face.text: It makes the scale start on a black key.

options.reason: The scale still starts on G, a white key. The F♯ comes near the top and fixes the pattern there.

face.text: It makes the step from E a [[tone|tone]] and the last step a [[semitone|semitone]].

questions.prompt: Which clip is the proper G major scale?
questions.hint: A major scale sounds bright all the way up. Listen for a note near the start that sounds darker.

options.reason: Clip A has a third note that is dropped too low, which makes the start sound darker and sadder. Clip B sounds bright all the way up.

points: G major is the major scale pattern started on G. It needs one sharp, F♯, to make the last two steps fit.
A [[key|key]] is the home set of notes a piece is built on. A piece that uses the notes of G major is in the key of G major.
A [[key-signature|key signature]] writes the sharps or flats once, at the start of the [[stave|stave]]. No signs means C major. One sharp, F♯, means G major, and every F is sharp.
